items.claim: A server-side request that reaches the metadata endpoint yields tokens minted for the VM's managed identity, so the impact of that SSRF is credential takeover of every identity attached to the VM rather than plain information disclosure.
items.body:

HackTricks reference: Cloud SSRF (pentesting-web/ssrf-server-side-request-forgery/cloud-ssrf.md)
items.disproof: Refuted if the metadata request from the SSRF sink returns no token, or hands back a token naming an identity that is not attached to the target VM and is rejected when used.

sources.quote:
Which basically means that you can impersonate all the managed identities attached to a VM.
>
> When requesting an access token to the metadata endpoint, by default the metadata service will use the system assigned managed identity to generate the token, if there is any system assigned managed identity.
As a result, the attacker can bypass access controls (such as firewalls) or hide the source of malicious requests, since the requests would not be coming directly from the attacker.

items.claim: When a VM has several user-assigned managed identities and no system-assigned one, the metadata service errors out instead of issuing a token, so identity enumeration has to pivot to the platform configuration endpoint to learn which identities exist.

items.claim: Blind SSRF escalates to exfiltration without ever seeing the raw HTTP body by pointing the URL at a benign text endpoint and then looking for that fetched text reproduced inside the downstream artifact the tester can actually read.
items.body:
Blind SSRF escalates to exfiltration without ever seeing the raw HTTP body by pointing the URL at a benign text endpoint and then looking for that fetched text reproduced inside the downstream artifact the tester can actually read.

HackTricks reference: SSRF Vulnerable Platforms (pentesting-web/ssrf-server-side-request-forgery/ssrf-vulnerable-platforms.md)
items.disproof: Refuted if the final artifact is byte-identical whether the callback URL is tester-controlled or replaced with an unreachable one, or the fetched body is never stored or re-rendered anywhere visible.

sources.quote:
1. confirm blind SSRF with OAST
2. point the URL to a harmless text endpoint such as https://icanhazip.com
3. force the downstream processor to treat the response as text (for example mime_type=text/plain)
4. look for the fetched response rendered inside the final artifact (generated image, OCR text, preview, moderation output, LLM response, PDF, etc.)

This turns a blind callback into response exfiltration without ever receiving the raw HTTP body directly.
